metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Cooper v. Oklahoma

Opinion filed: 1996-04-23

Docket No.: 95-5207

Citations:
• 134 L. Ed. 2d 498
• 116 S. Ct. 1373
• 517 U.S. 348
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 2649

Case holding summaries:
• finding Oklahoma statute that required defendant to prove incompetence by "clear and convincing" rather than a "more likely than not" preponderance standard was too demanding and therefore unconstitutional
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• rejecting -12- Oklahoma’s requirement that a defendant prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• holding statute which presumed defendant was competent to stand trial and must prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence created unconstitutional risk that defendant would be put to trial even if he was, more likely than not, incompetent
• finding Oklahoma's clear and convincing standard governing post-examination competency hearings "incompatible with the dictates of due process"
• holding statute which presumed defendant was competent to stand trial and must prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence created unconstitutional risk that defendant would be put to trial even if he was, more likely than not, incompetent
• "[D]ue process requires at a minimum a showing that the person is mentally ill and either poses a danger to himself or others or is incapable of 'surviving safely in freedom.'"
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• in turn quoting Dusky v. United States, 362 U.S. 402, 80 S.Ct. 788, 4 L.Ed.2d 824 (1960)
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• emphasizing that a critical component of competence is the ability to "communicate effectively with defense counsel"
• "Congress has directed that the accused in a federal prosecution must prove incompetence by a preponderance of the evidence."
• preponderance standard governs the decision once competence has been drawn into question
• holding the Oklahoma requirement that defendant prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence, rather than by a preponderance of the evidence, violates due process
• “We have repeatedly and consistently recognized that the criminal trial of an incompetent defendant violates due process.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "Congress has directed that the accused in a federal prosecution must prove incompetence by a preponderance of the evidence."
• "The right not to stand trial while incompetent is sufficiently important to merit protection even if the defendant has failed to make a timely request for a competency determination."
• government cannot prosecute if defendant shows he is “more likely than not” in‐ competent
• finding due process violation in a rule having no common-law pedigree whatever, and adopted, very recently, by only four States
• "[a] heightened standard [of proof] does not decrease the risk of error, but simply reallocates that risk between the parties"
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• "Congress has directed that the accused in a federal prosecution must prove incompetence by a preponderance of the evidence."
• noting that "the State's interest in the efficient operation of its criminal justice system" is an "important state interest[]"
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• explaining how the consequences of an erroneous determination threaten the fundamental fairness of our criminal justice system
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• “Indeed, the right not to stand trial while incompetent is sufficiently important to merit protection even if the defendant has failed to make a timely request for a competency determination.”
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• "Congress has directed that the accused in a federal prosecution must prove incompetence by a preponderance of the evidence."
• holding that state law presuming criminal defendant is competent to stand trial unless he proves incompetence by clear and convincing evidence violates Due Process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• “A heightened standard [of proof] does not decrease the risk of error, but simply reallocates that risk between the parties.”
• “We have repeatedly and consistently recognized that ‘the criminal trial of an incompetent defendant violates due process.’”
• holding that state law requiring defendant to prove incompetence to stand trial by clear-and-convincing evidence violated the Due Process Clause
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• "We do not think the Code of Criminal Procedure has made any radical change in the mode of procedure or the character of the [competency] proceedings"
• the court "was familiar with the appearance and conduct of the prisoner during the period of that trial, and had sufficient grounds before it to judge as to the probability of his present sanity"
• states may require the accused to prove his incompetency to stand trial only by a preponderance of the evidence; a higher standard of "clear and convincing evidence" violates the Due Process Clause
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• criminal trial of incompetent defendant violates due process
• noting that the Supreme Court has "repeatedly and consistently recognized that `the criminal trial of an incompetent defendant violates due process'" (quoting Medina v. California, 505 U.S. 437, 453, 112 S.Ct. 2572, 120 L.Ed.2d 353 (1992))
• holding that Oklahoma's requirement that a defendant prove his incompetency by clear and convincing evidence violated due process
• in upholding Oklahoma statute that presumed a defendant competent unless he rebutted the presumption, Supreme Court commented that under § 4241 "Congress has directed that the accused in a federal prosecution must prove incompetence by a preponderance of the evidence"
• holding statute which presumed defendant was competent to stand trial and must prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence created unconstitutional risk that defendant would be put to trial even if he was, more likely than not, incompetent
